AI adoption grows in Asia, but measuring the gains remains tricky
headlines.summary: Businesses across Asia-Pacific are seeing returns from AI investments, even as confidence in measuring those gains varies, according to an AWS survey.
headlines.article_text: AI adoption grows in Asia, but measuring the gains remains tricky Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Some 58% of businesses using AI said their investments had surpassed initial costs, according to an AWS survey. More businesses are moving AI projects from experimentation into production, AWS executive Jaime Vallés told CNBC. A shortage of AI and digital skills remains a key barrier, cited by 48% of businesses, according to the survey. In this article AMZN Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT An Amazon Web Services AI data center in New Carlisle, Indiana, on Oct. 2, 2025. Noah Berger | Getty Images Businesses across Asia-Pacific say their investments in artificial intelligence are paying off, with the technology helping boost productivity and revenue. But putting a number on those gains is proving far less straightforward. Some 58% of businesses using AI said their investments had already surpassed their initial costs, yet just 12% were very confident in their ability to accurately measure their return on investment, according to research conducted by Strand Partners for Amazon Web Services . APAC, to make it simpler, has all the ingredients to be in my view the core or the center of worldwide innovation. Jaime Vallés VP, Amazon Web Services The survey included 9,750 business leaders across 10 Asia-Pacific markets: Australia, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, New Zealand, the Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam. The biggest shift over the past year has been the growing number of companies moving AI projects into production, Jaime Vallés, AWS vice president for Asia Pacific, Japan and China, told CNBC in an exclusive interview. "From year over year, probably the biggest difference is you're seeing a lot of ideas put into production," Vallés said. From pilots to results Despite the reported financial benefits, many businesses remain in the early stages of AI adoption. The survey found that 64% of businesses using AI across Asia-Pacific and Japan still rely on general-purpose AI tools or ready-made solutions for specific tasks, while only 19% of businesses have a formal and comprehensive AI strategy. Among those with such an AI strategy, 35% had reached the most advanced stage of adoption, compared with just 8% of businesses without one, according to the research. Technology alone is not enough to turn AI investments into meaningful business outcomes, Vallés said. He pointed to what he called the "four Rs of readiness": technological, cultural, skills and personal readiness. "Where we see more meaningful impact is when you see the leadership using AI, building a culture of using AI and using AI to transform and not automate," Vallés said. Financial services is among the sectors seeing stronger AI adoption. Vallés pointed to Vietnam's Techcombank as an example, saying the bank is using AI to assess loan applications and expand access to credit for small businesses. The technology has helped the bank to analyze more data and approve some loan applications that might otherwise have been rejected, he said. Techcombank, one of Vietnam's largest commercial banks, serves more than 16.5 million retail and corporate customers. According to an AWS case study , its modernization of digital banking infrastructure using AWS improved application response times by up to 35% and cut the time needed to launch new product features by 30%. What's next for Asia? AI adoption continued to expand across Asia-Pacific, with all 10 markets surveyed recording increases from the previous year. Australia led the group with an adoption rate of 61%, followed by Singapore at 59% and South Korea at 58%. Still, businesses face significant obstacles to scaling AI investments. A shortage of AI and digital skills remains a key barrier, cited by 48% of respondents as an obstacle to adoption or expansion. Despite those challenges, Vallés expressed optimism about Asia-Pacific's role in AI innovation, pointing to the region's cultural diversity and range of perspectives. "I am convinced that most of the innovation in the fullness of time will come from our region," he said. Vallés added that Asia-Pacific has the ingredients to become a global center for innovation, citing its diversity, talent, startup ecosystem and technology. "APAC, to make it simpler, has all the ingredients to be in my view the core or the center of worldwide innovation," he said. Governments across Asia also play a role in supporting Al adoption and addressing barriers to its wider use. About 72% of government respondents said Al had increased productivity, according to a report released by the Pacific Economic Cooperation Council in November, which surveyed more than 500 experts across 23 Asia-Pacific economies. Around 59% of respondents viewed government support as a moderately or very important factor in accelerating AI adoption next year, though existing regulations were also seen as a constraint, the report showed. Such support is also taking share through regional cooperation. The Asian Development Bank and South Korea established a $20 million fund to help developing economies adopt Al and address gaps in digital skills and infrastructure, according to an announcement by the bank earlier this month. headlines.article_text: Amazon faces FAA probe after delivery drone strikes Michigan garage Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points The FAA said it will investigate an Amazon drone crash near Detroit, Michigan. An Amazon spokesperson told CNBC there were no injuries and the drone has been removed. Amazon has been working to make drone delivery a reality for nearly 13 years. In this article AMZN Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Amazon's new MK30 Prime Air drone is displayed during Amazon's "Delivering the Future" event at the company's BFI1 Fulfillment Center, Robotics Research and Development Hub in Sumner, Washington on Oct. 18, 2023. Jason Redmond | AFP | Getty Images The Federal Aviation Administration said Monday it will investigate a recent Amazon drone crash near Detroit. On Friday, one of Amazon's MK30 drones "landed on a resident's garage" during a delivery in Huntington Woods, Michigan, a suburb north of Detroit, Amazon spokesperson Jack Stelzner told CNBC in a statement. The crash occurred after the drone dropped off a customer's shampoo order around 4:30 p.m. local time, and one of its propellers was damaged in the incident, according to ABC affiliate WXYZ . A preliminary incident report posted to the FAA's website states the drone "struck a fiber cable, a residential garage, and became entangled in power lines during takeoff." The report says the condition of the drone is unknown. Stelzner said there were no injuries, the drone has been removed and Amazon is in contact with the resident. "Safety is our top priority and incidents are extremely rare," Stelzner said. "Anytime a delivery does not go as planned we investigate what happened and use the findings to further improve the service." An FAA spokesperson confirmed it's investigating the incident. A spokesperson for the National Transportation Safety Board, a federal agency that also investigates aviation accidents, said it's aware of the incident and is continuing to gather information. The agency hasn't yet determined whether it will open a probe, the NTSB spokesperson added. Amazon has been working to make widespread drone delivery a reality ever since founder Jeff Bezos laid out his vision for the program nearly 13 years ago. The rollout has been slow, as the program encountered regulatory delays and staff cuts , as well as technical challenges and pushback from some communities where it conducted early pilots. Expansion has recently ramped up. The company is targeting a launch of its drone service in 500 U.S. cities and towns by the end of the year, while an Amazon executive claimed it has the "highest demand drone delivery service in the industry," CNBC previously reported . The e-commerce giant has encountered some challenges along the way. Federal investigators opened a probe nearly one year ago after an Amazon drone downed an internet cable in Waco, Texas. One month earlier, a separate federal probe was opened into an incident near Phoenix, where two Amazon drones collided with a construction crane.
